lines.text: The hospital kept lamps lit for the arrivals last night. I took clean blankets over.
The laundry line has become a second village wall. At least this one is soft.
The Academy has another pupil. I hope somebody shows them which door opens onto the yard.
A first bowl of ramen should come with a lesson on where to put the elbows.
Practice falls sound different from real ones. Usually there is more arguing afterwards.
The training post has acquired a chalk face. Apparently it needed an expression for losing.
The Academy pupils are practising their control. I have never seen so much attention paid to a leaf.
A leaf balanced on a brow looks very scholarly until somebody sneezes.
The watch is checking the lanes after dark. Let them work, and keep your lamps where they can be seen.
Somebody accused my laundry of being a figure on the roof. A rather well-dressed figure, I thought.
The library is busy with Academy work. Return what you borrow before the next class needs it.
There is a new bookmark by the catalogue. It says to stop using the catalogue as a bookmark.
Study groups have been carrying food through the Academy streets all afternoon.
Exam preparation apparently requires enough rice to support a small bridge.
New forehead protectors in the street today. The pupils keep touching them to make sure they stay.
A polished forehead protector can reflect a very worried face. I recommended breakfast first.
The new squads have their assignments. Three young voices make a surprisingly large discussion.
The new squad tried walking through the tea-house door together. The door voted for single file.
Small errands keep the village moving. A delivered parcel matters most to the person waiting for it.
A new Genin asked whether carrying turnips counted as training. The grower provided a second basket.
The training trees are busy. Give the students room when you pass underneath.
I watched somebody climb halfway up a trunk and remember gravity with great conviction.
The gate watch is checking cart loads more carefully. Leave extra time for deliveries.
The tea-house keeper wants a cart without squeaking wheels. I suggested a cart without tea cups first.
The lake drills have begun. Dry towels have become the most popular training equipment.
A student assured me the splash was deliberate. A very thorough demonstration of water.
Some missions send the young squads farther from home. I packed food that keeps on the road.
The map shop has a notice asking people to unfold the map before complaining about the missing river.
The desk has named the road threat: Yūgure. Read the notice rather than spreading a different version.
The gate clerk keeps a spare pencil on a string. The string has outlasted three pencils and two arguments.
Exam candidates are arriving with their papers. Point visitors towards the hall if they ask.
The proctors borrowed extra ink. That sounds more frightening than borrowing extra targets.
The forest stage is under way. The adults outside the fence look less patient than the candidates did.
Someone packed a bedroll so tightly that opening it counted as the first survival exercise.
The placement bouts are finished. A judges' note can say more than a cheer if you read it properly.
One spectator attempted to explain footwork while standing on a dropped rice ball.
There is time for training before the finals. There should also be time for eating and mending straps.
The tailors can recognise an exam candidate by the new patch over the old patch.
The stadium is closed after the attack. Leave the stair clear for the people bringing help.
The relief kitchen has labelled the onions very firmly. Even in this mess, somebody keeps putting them with the pears.
The promotion notices are up. Some of those new Chunin were pupils only a short time ago.
A new vest arrived with three people offering to explain its pockets. The wearer needed lunch more urgently.
You chose a game piece for the offcut. I kept the darker grain as the top.
You made the scrap a cup rest. Somebody has already put it to work.
You wanted the bench facing the path. I left room for people to stop and talk.
You chose the river view. I checked how the seat dries in the morning.
You chose another measurement. The piece fitted without the small argument I expected.
You wanted a practice piece. It became the pattern for the second one.
You wanted the useful gift chosen together. The handle fits the person who will use it.
You chose the surprise. I watched what the person kept borrowing before starting.
You wanted the repair visible. I chose wood that made the patch easy to find.
You chose a quiet repair. It holds without asking anyone to notice.
You joined the loud table. There was room for your story between the serving bowls.
You wanted the quiet corner. I left the small table where the door stays open.
You trusted the good tool to another pair of hands. They brought it back carefully.
You chose the spare for learning. The first mistake did not end the lesson.
You wanted the crooked leg fixed. The table stopped teaching everyone to balance their cups.
You left the harmless crooked part for later. We got the urgent repair finished first.
You chose the sound of cooking. I thought of that while carrying bowls into the yard.
You chose the sound of nearby work. I left the door open while I sanded.
You wanted the maker remembered. I added the apprentice's mark beside the master's.
You thought the lasting thing could be enough. I watched somebody use the bench without asking who made it.
A cup rest. I spill less when the table has somewhere for everything.
Halfway between. I would like to see who is arriving.
Both when the wood belongs to somebody else.
Ask one question, then keep a small part as the surprise.
Visible if it tells the next person how to fix it again.
A corner near the noise. I like knowing everybody is there.
The spare first, then the good one when we both know the grip.
I check what is holding the weight. Appearance can wait for safety.
A chair moving to make space at the table.
A little mark, so an apprentice knows another pair of hands learned this once.
Mind the shavings. I am making a very small mess with a very large broom.
Sit here. I checked the leg. That bench over there is still a theory.
Mum packed extra. I think she counts my whole class as a visitor.
Oh, good. Hold this straight edge a moment, {player}.
At our table the serving bowl goes round twice. The second time is for people who were being polite.
If I mark where my foot lands, I can see the mistake. Like measuring a crooked shelf.
This offcut could be a cup rest. Or a smaller offcut. I am deciding.
Our yard sounds like work even when everyone is eating. Somebody always taps the table to test it.
A good joint is the bit nobody notices because it keeps holding.
Put a support under the heavy end before you try lifting it.
I would like to build a place people still use when nobody remembers who built it.
Making a thing takes so much longer than breaking it. I keep making them.
We can eat by the river. I fixed the handle on the basket.
The lid becomes a little table. Here, this is the clever part.
There. We found a use for that scrap of wood and an entire afternoon.
The form held! I had to think of it as a frame with moving corners.
That did not fit. I will measure the gap before I cut the next piece.
You chose to walk beside me. I stopped getting a whole pace ahead.
You wanted somebody watching ahead. I kept close enough to hear you.
You watched the lead foot. Your correction made the turn quieter.
You chose the following foot. I had not noticed how often it dragged.
You chose the platform. I checked which boards keep the evening chill.
You wanted the riverbank. The reflection stayed longer than the moon between the clouds.
You wanted openings called early. I started hearing where my guard had already moved.
You chose to compare after the strike. We had noticed different parts of the same turn.
You asked me to check the knot. I liked that neither of us had to pretend it was an insult.
You wanted to show the knot yourself. I waited, and you found the twist.
You wanted a visible place to wait. I stood where the bend opens.
You chose to walk back. The path felt shorter with somebody returning along it.
You chose the weak form. It stopped being the one you avoided.
You wanted the form you enjoy. I noticed how much steadier it made your next attempt.
You wanted a quiet warning. I got close enough to give it before the drill started.
You wanted the warning clear to everyone. We changed the drill together.
You said the quiet watch counted. I stopped apologising for having no exciting report.
You thought a quiet watch could teach. I started keeping track of the ordinary sounds.
You chose the promise you could keep. I have been trying to make mine clear and possible.
You wanted the difficult promise made honestly. I said what I could not guarantee.
Side by side when the path allows it. I can see you without turning.
The following one. It tells me whether the person can change their mind.
The platform, with a clear way down before we get sleepy.
Before when teaching. After when we both need to learn.
No. I would rather have the knot hold than have my pride hold.
Walk back, unless moving would make us lose each other.
The weak form, then one I know. I like ending with my feet sure.
Quiet if it is a correction. Loud if somebody is about to get hurt.
Yes. I want the people passing to be bored enough to stop looking over their shoulders.
I ask what the person needs before choosing how brave I want to sound.
I checked the path. You can put your pack here.
Left foot first today. Watch it, {player}. Tell me if I favour it.
The training ground is clear. I left room for another stance.
Your strap is loose. Let me hold the buckle while you tighten it.
Something I can eat without taking my eyes off the yard. I am working on sitting down properly.
An opening is a direction you forgot to watch. I am learning to watch more than one.
I oil the scabbard before the moon-viewing walk. Quiet work suits the evening.
My sibling checks my knots when I am not looking. I leave one easy to check.
Say which side you need covered. I would rather be useful than guessed at.
Tell the person beside you what you are about to do. A warning can be a kindness.
A guard post where the people passing can afford to stop watching the road.
Sometimes I check an exit twice. I am trying to make the second look quicker.
A few rounds? Footwork first. I want you watching my balance.
I will call the opening after the strike. Tell me if I saw the same one you did.
Your step made me change mine. That is a useful afternoon.
I passed the form. My hands stayed steady after the first mistake.
I hesitated in practice. Good place to find it. I will try again.
Feet set. Watch the hands.
Your opening is closing.
Need a moment. Cover the gap.
Keep them covered. I am moving.
Get clear. Count everyone.
Tools down. We heard the yield.
Back by the route we checked.
Count heads before tools.
We are clear. Find the injured first.
Too much weight on that side.
Read it. Change the angle.
Good opening. Use the space.
Clear my line.
Change the shape. Less chakra.
Something moved twice. Check it.
Found the seam. Eyes open.
Smoke. Stay within voice range.
Keep moving. The decoy bought one step.
Wait for my turn. Now.
Your nature first. I will build on it.
Hold still. Breathe normally.
Taking the opening.
I have this side.
Moving with you.
Holding this patch of ground.
On the signal.
Um. I can see the gap from here.
This way. The empty space is not empty.
I need a little cover. Please.
I can keep that corner hidden. Go.
Sorry. The line went out of reach.
They stopped. Please do not strike again.
The path behind us is still clear.
We are all here. I checked.
Could we sit somewhere without all that noise?
I saw the line before it reached me.
Oh. That angle was different.
It joined up. Did you see?
Watch the edge of the shape.
That one blurred. I will change it.
The colours repeat. That is wrong.
There. The real shadow has an edge.
Smoke makes softer edges. Stay near.
Only a decoy. I am over here.
I will leave an opening for your next step.
Your colour first. Mine can follow it.
Hold this cloth here. Gently.
Yes. I can reach that gap.
I can cover this edge.
Right beside your shadow.
Um. This spot. Got it.
Ready for your first move.
With me! The pup has already voted!
Hey! Try catching the noisy one!
Still here! Could use a hand, though!
Cover that side! I am going in for them!
Okay... floor first... getting up later...
Stop swinging! They said enough!
Back this way! Nobody wanders off!
All of us standing! That is the good bit!
Next time we fix that gap first. All of us.
Ha! Saw your foot move!
Right! Less shouting, quicker hands!
That is where the whole drill goes!
Give me room for the loud part!
Fine! I have another way in!
Wait. Why is the pup in two places?
One pup! Much better!
Smoke out! Follow my incredibly useful voice!
Missed! I am the one still moving!
Give me the opening and I will take it!
Your turn, then mine! Make it big!
Stay put! I brought the bandages this time!
Right! Opening coming up!
Nobody past this bit!
With you! Watch the pup!
Staying put! Somehow!
Our turn! Give the signal!
Make the first attempt count.
You left that side open twice.
The stance holds. I need a moment.
Cover the fallen one. Stop staring.
That... was a clean opening.
Enough. I know when the form is broken.
This ground is spent. Move.
Now show me you can do it twice.
I saw the fault. Leave me room to fix it.
Your wrist announced that.
An angle I have not practised. Yet.
That opening was earned.
Watch carefully if you want to learn.
Then I change the approach.
A borrowed picture. Find the boundary.
Your illusion lost its balance.
Smoke. Change position before it thins.
You committed to the decoy.
You chose to ask about the form. I have changed the instruction that made you stop.
You wanted time to read. The chair beside the desk proved more useful than another notice.
You chose the direct garden path. I asked the gardener where the roots needed space.
You wanted the path round the tree. We put a seat at the bend.
You wanted the place saved. The visitor sat without losing the turn they had waited for.
You chose the chair. It now stays beside the queue instead of in a locked room.
You wanted the seal explained first. The visitor knew what the document would change.
You chose to hear the whole paper. The final condition deserved its own question.
You chose another gentle offer. Our guest asked for water once the question became smaller.
You wanted the cup left within reach. Our guest used it without another explanation.
You wanted the small obstacle removed promptly. We kept the desk open for the new questions.
You chose to hear the quiet visitors first. Their objection was not the one we had expected.
You wanted the full words kept. They settled a disagreement about what had actually been promised.
You chose decisions with reasons. We added the question that had not yet been settled.
You wanted both neighbours heard together. We began by agreeing whose turn came first.
You chose separate first accounts. We asked permission before bringing their words to the same table.
You wanted the person's name beside the number. The new cover leaves enough room for it.
You wanted us to ask how the visitor wished to be called. I added that question before opening the file.
You meant a place where things could be found. The new labels passed their first visitor's test.
You called a thing in order when people could use it. I have stopped treating a full desk as proof of failure.
Read it, then ask about the sentence that seemed simple on the first pass.
The way a tired visitor can actually walk, whatever the drawing prefers.
A chair and a saved place. We need not make comfort compete with fairness.
The whole paper, with permission to interrupt before we reach the seal.
A cup nearby, and a person who remains available.
Hear enough to understand the obstacle, then give the change a date.
Decisions, reasons, and a way to consult the fuller record.
Separately if someone is afraid. Procedure must be able to notice that.
A name the person recognises, and a number the clerks can put in order.
Usable. I keep reminding my household that I said so.
{player}. The forms are in order. I hope your breakfast was as well.
Come in. The queue can spare a moment for the person holding the paper.
A signature can wait while you catch your breath.
You have a question. Good. A blank form is a poor listener.
The household argues over pickles more fiercely than the council argues over paths.
A schedule should leave time to mend the sandal that schedule wore through.
The garden keeps its own agenda. I enjoy being overruled by a bean plant.
My household has several opinions about when a guest has had enough tea. You need not agree with any.
A rule is not doing its work if the people it serves cannot explain it.
Ask to read the condition before agreeing to it. We can wait while you do.
A registry that welcomes a child before asking which house sent them.
I keep a second chair beside the desk. It reminds me to hear a person, rather than a file.
There is shade beside the garden. We may leave the files indoors.
These shoots need space. Advice I should remember at the council table.
An afternoon with no seal required. We should put that in good order more often.
Your lesson is complete. Tell me what made the last attempt different.
There is no penalty for asking which part of the instruction was unclear.
You preferred arriving early. I had the papers ready before the bell.
You chose the bell as your measure. The appointment began when you said it would.
You chose to copy the uncertain letters. The gaps were more useful than guesses.
You read the whole line before copying. You caught the date the single letters had concealed.
You wanted a separate spare key. You remembered not to put both on the same ring.
You chose a trusted keeper for the spare. The arrangement was clear before it was needed.
You read the margin note as a clue. You also checked whose hand had left it.
You set the margin aside until you understood the entry. The second reading changed its meaning.
You chose a careful rubbing. The faint line remained where the eye had lost it.
You copied only what you could see. Another reader could tell exactly where the uncertainty began.
You asked the difficult question first. We had to return to the date before the answer made sense.
You began with what was certain. Your final question was shorter and harder to evade.
You wanted the error visible beneath the correction. The next reader could follow both hands.
You chose the dated note. That gave the next reader a way to check the change.
You chose a bounded wait. The late visitor found somebody still expecting them.
You wanted word sent. There was a useful reason for the delay, as there often is.
You wanted the crease mentioned without humiliation. The borrower asked how to protect the next page.
You chose the quiet repair. The binding needed attention more than the reader did.
You thought patience could mean leaving room. I let the answer arrive without another question.
You called patience a kind of attention. You noticed the page was difficult to turn.
Early. There is nearly always a stair somebody else needs first.
The line first, then every letter. Neither is allowed to excuse the other.
A spare in a known place, with a person who knows why it is there.
Evidence that somebody else read the page. What it proves requires more work.
Both, with permission. Different records can correct each other.
The facts first. I distrust the shape of a question I have not examined.
A dated correction, with the source beside it. Ink is not proof by itself.
Send word, and leave the appointment open until I know what happened.
Find the cause before choosing whom to instruct.
Attention. Waiting without it can become another way of looking away.
You are early. Remain so.
Keep the path clear, child. People use it even when you cannot see them.
A question may wait until the bell has finished.
You have brought mud to a stone path. An achievement of sorts.
Tea without crumbs in the records room. The crumbs are more persistent than children.
Put a tool back in the same place. You should not have to search in the dark.
Old handwriting rewards patience. Hurry, and every letter becomes the one you expected.
My teacher expected punctuality. I have found no reason to lower the standard.
An entry without a date is a rumour with tidy handwriting.
Write the question down before you ask it. You may discover which answer you fear.
Records that can be understood without their keeper standing beside the desk.
A mislaid key makes everyone wait. I account for mine before leaving.
Walk the shrine path if you wish. Leave the lanterns where they are.
Read the weathered line slowly. The stone has already waited this long.
You stayed until the last line. Few do.
A completed exercise belongs in its proper folder. Pride is no filing system.
Copy it again tomorrow, child. A tired hand merely copies its own errors.
You chose a place near the food. I trusted you with the bowl that has to reach everybody.
You wanted a place near the talk. I noticed you made room for the quiet guest.
You saved the extra bun. I put a cloth beside the basket this time.
You chose to share the extra. Somebody at the far table stopped pretending not to be hungry.
You wanted the meeting to pause for food. We agreed faster when we came back.
You wanted the last point finished. I kept the next matter for another day.
You chose to follow the recipe. The kitchen has an actual record of what worked.
You wanted to taste along the way. The onions escaped my usual enthusiasm.
You wanted the new arrival shown around. You remembered where the confusing turn was.
You chose a seat before the tour. Our guest asked the first question without being hurried.
You wanted the desk brought closer to the child. The conversation became easier to hear.
You chose the taller chair. I asked for steps before somebody tried the drawer handles.
You thanked the cook. The kitchen made enough for the person carrying it too.
You thanked the carrier. I followed the tray back to see who had filled it.
You wanted the rule explained. The question showed us a needless step.
You chose simpler wording. A visitor filled the form without help today.
You wanted the quiet speaker given time. We heard the answer that was waiting behind the pause.
You chose to offer a starting point. Our guest found a different answer and said it.
You wanted us to ask who was missing. We found a person the invitation had passed by.
You wanted to ask the people already there. The smallest suggestion changed the room.
Near whoever has not been asked anything yet.
Share it, then ask the kitchen whether later has been provided for.
A break before we start mistaking tiredness for conviction.
Follow it once. Then ask the person eating whether the recipe knew enough.
A seat, a cup, then a person who has time to walk beside them.
I would come round the desk. Furniture can wait for the carpenter.
Both, and whoever washed the pan. Gratitude has a longer route than the tray.
Explain it to the person who will live under it, and listen to the questions.
Wait a little. Then ask whether help would make the question smaller.
Keep asking. A room can be welcoming on one day and difficult on another.
Come closer, little one. That chair is for sitting in, even with muddy sandals.
There is room at this table. There is always room if we move the paperwork.
A quick visit? Then a small bun. We have negotiated.
You look busy. Sit long enough to tell me what filled the morning.
A kitchen that knows how much to make also knows who has not come home yet.
You can learn a great deal carrying the cooking pot together. Especially when somebody walks too fast.
I try a recipe when the paperwork gets stubborn. The recipe usually cooperates.
My daughter runs a better kitchen than I do. Please do not report that I admitted it.
If a child needs three forms to ask for lunch, the forms need changing.
Start by asking who will have to live with the decision after you leave the room.
An orphan arriving at any gate should know there is a bed already waiting.
A long table can still leave somebody at the end unheard. I try to walk round it.
The kitchen has a table free. Let us improve that situation.
Turn that piece now. Leading a village has not taught me to stop burning onions.
A useful meeting. We settled lunch before it became a committee.
A lesson passed deserves a meal with the people who helped. Take enough for them.
An exam is a morning. You have many mornings left to grow into.
You asked to see it first. I have moved the demonstration so you can see both hands.
You wanted the first try. I saved the blank half of the board for it.
You chose the window. I kept the chalk dust away from that desk.
You wanted the front row. This drawing is especially ready for your criticism.
You picked a sweet study snack. I brought enough to share this time.
You wanted a filling snack. The rice balls are beside the homework.
You chose your partner. I made the exercise need both of your ideas.
You tried a new partner. I noticed you made room at the desk afterwards.
You defended the funny drawing. It now has labels, so we can call it scholarship.
You asked for a clearer diagram. I practised until the target stopped looking edible.
You wanted to talk the problem through. I will listen before reaching for the chalk.
You asked for quiet thinking time. This desk is free until the bell.
You chose the clear mark. I left space beside it for your own explanation.
You asked for notes. I kept this one short enough to fit beside the actual mistake.
You wanted to show the correction beside the mistake. A younger pupil tried the same idea today.
You wanted time before sharing your practice page. I have not shown it to anyone.
You voted for the game. I made sure watching counts as taking part.
You wanted the exhibition. I left a space for the first attempt beside each final piece.
You said one new thing makes a lesson worthwhile. What was today's thing?
You wanted a lesson where asking felt safe. We can start with the question you saved.
I need to try it, then ask why my demonstration has become a broom.
By the door, so I notice anyone trying to come in quietly.
Whatever does not leave fingerprints on the answer sheet.
Somebody new. Teachers need practice meeting people too.
Keep it if you remember the lesson. Otherwise the potato retires.
Explaining it aloud. The empty classroom is an excellent, patient pupil.
A note. Mine usually starts with: slow down.
Yes. I have enough examples to supply several classes.
A game with an exhibition attached. This is why I need pupils to stop me.
When a pupil asks the question the rest were holding back.
There you are! I saved the example with the least embarrassing drawing.
A question before class? Wonderful. A question about lunch? Also wonderful.
Left foot looking steadier, {player}! Yes, I notice these things.
Come in! A classroom can fit one more question.
A proper lunch has something besides the thing you traded three rice balls for.
You missed the mark. Tell me which part nearly worked, and we start there.
I keep a list of things each pupil does well. Some pages need extra paper.
My mother sells pickles. She thinks a flak vest is an expensive apron.
A quiet pupil still has a question. My job is to leave room for it.
Try the smallest part you can do today. Tomorrow gets its own attempt.
A school where asking for help feels as ordinary as asking for chalk.
Sometimes I fill a silence too quickly. I am practising waiting.
Bring the exercise you keep folding out of sight. That one, yes!
Slow it down until you can tell me where your fingers lose the shape.
Look at that margin! Three tries, and three different corrections. That is studying.
You passed the lesson! Tell me which correction helped. I am writing it down.
A failed attempt is a useful page. We will put the next one beside it.
You preferred the ribbon bookmark. I tied one where it would not strain the binding.
You chose the paper slip. The question on it helped find where we stopped.
You chose the window. I moved the chair before the afternoon glare arrived.
You preferred the lamp. I left the safer shade beside your table.
You wanted the title first. You found the neighbouring volume without my help.
You chose to browse. That unexpected shelf answered a better question.
You chose a silent first reading. The second one let you hear the rhythm for yourself.
You asked to hear the passage. The punctuation finally sounded like advice.
You wanted a clean copy. We compared the edition before trusting the fresh cover.
You chose the annotated book. Finding its reader became part of understanding the page.
You chose the ending first. You saw the small promise in the opening paragraph.
You wanted the journey. I stopped myself from pointing at the final shelf mark.
You wanted the note to stay near the passage. I made a sleeve so it could be removed safely.
You brought the note to the desk. Its writer had remembered the words and forgotten the page.
You marked the doubtful part in your notes. It was easy to check when we found another source.
You wanted another reader for the doubtful line. The disagreement made us check the date.
You shared your favourite. Your explanation found a reader the catalogue would have missed.
You chose a book for the reader. The small question you asked mattered more than the shelf mark.
You put the difficult book aside. I kept the bookmark so returning would be easy.
You chose one paragraph instead of the whole book. We understood it well enough to ask about the next.
Paper, because I am always writing questions I cannot finish at the desk.
The window until the weather changes, then a lamp and an unreasonable number of notes.
The catalogue, followed by the shelf beside the one I intended.
Aloud, softly. I find the sentence I thought I understood was missing a word.
The old one, with the clean one beside it if I can carry both.
The journey. Though I have been known to check whether the animal gets home.
The desk first. We can keep a copy beside the passage if the writer agrees.
On my notes, with a reason. Otherwise tomorrow I am only arguing with yesterday's punctuation.
One for their question, and my favourite if they have room in the bag.
One paragraph, then permission to stop. Understanding is poor work when it becomes punishment.
The shelf ladder is occupied. By books, mostly. I am negotiating.
You may sit by the window. Turn the page before you move the chair.
A book for today, {player}, or a question that needs several?
There is a bookmark on the desk. You need not fold that corner.
Lunch stays outside the reading room. A surprising number of pupils believe sauce can be a bookmark.
The index is a technique too. Learn it, and you can find the exercise without practising every page.
I copy interesting handwriting. The untidy ones take more practice than you would think.
My grandmother repaired torn pages with rice paste. I still make too much at once.
Write where you found it. Another reader should be able to walk the same path.
Read the sentence before the one that frightened you. And the one after.
A library where a child can reach the first shelf without asking permission.
I sometimes answer the question I expected instead of the one you asked. Please correct me.
The quiet table is free. We can each bring something unfinished.
That margin note is a question. The next reader answered it a year later.
We did not finish the stack. A good reason to leave the bookmark where it is.
You found the passage yourself. Keep the shelf mark; remembering where is half the work.
A wrong answer with a source can be checked. Bring both, and we will start there.
You asked for reminders to drink. The cup still needs you to do the lifting.
You wanted the full cup where you could see it. I moved it away from the paper slips.
You chose the quiet room. I left a note so visitors knock softly.
You wanted the corridor sounds. I left the door open a little.
You asked for the proper term first. You explained it back without needing the long word.
You preferred the plain explanation. That helped the next patient understand it too.
You wanted neat folds. Your last crane stands without leaning on the jar.
You chose to finish the awkward crane. I kept it beside the tidy one.
You agreed to come early. We solved that one while it was still small.
You wanted clear signs to watch. You noticed the change instead of guessing.
You wanted quiet company. I brought work that does not need conversation.
You asked for a later visit. I returned at the time you chose.
You chose to keep your own notes. Your dates helped us see the pattern.
You left the record with me. I saved time for your corrections before closing the page.
You wanted the plan you could follow. Packed food turned out more useful than my beautiful timetable.
You asked to see the ideal as well. We marked the changes that were possible first.
